blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Extrusive volcanic landforms are created when lava cools on the Earth's surface, forming shield volcanoes, composite cones, calderas, and flood basalt plains.
Intrusive volcanic landforms result from magma cooling and solidifying beneath the Earth's crust, forming batholiths, laccoliths, lopoliths, phacoliths, sills, and dikes.
Batholiths are massive granitic intrusive bodies that represent cooled magma chambers exposed only after extensive surface erosion.
The Deccan Traps of India represent a premier example of a flood basalt province formed by intense volcanic fissure eruptions.

blocks.content: Calderas are the most explosive of the Earth's volcanoes, so violent that when they erupt, they tend to collapse on themselves rather than building any tall structure.

rows: On or above the Earth's surface

items: Distinction between Dikes and Sills: Dikes are near-vertical sheet-like magma intrusions, whereas Sills are horizontal magma sheets formed parallel to bedding planes.
Lava Viscosity Impact: Low-viscosity basaltic lava forms gently sloping shield volcanoes, whereas high-viscosity viscous lava forms steep, explosive composite volcanoes.
Deccan Traps: Questions frequently test the classification of Peninsular India's volcanic terrain as a Flood Basalt Province.
